questions.question: How does this async cloud coding agent differ architecturally from an interactive terminal coding agent?
options: The async agent uses a different LLM provider and does not support Python repositories
The trigger is a GitHub label; the agent runs non-interactively in a cloud sandbox, clones the repo, iterates without a human in the loop, and opens a PR when done
The async agent skips CI verification to reduce latency and opens a draft PR immediately
The async agent runs locally on the developer's machine rather than in a cloud sandbox
questions.explanation: The async cloud agent has no interactive terminal. A GitHub label triggers it; it spins up in a cloud sandbox, works autonomously through its agent loop, verifies CI in-sandbox, and opens a review-ready PR with rationale.

questions.question: What scope of GitHub App permissions does the agent use, and why are they kept minimal?
options: Full repository admin rights are required to run CI checks and push branches
Fine-grained installation token covering issues read+write, pull_requests write, contents read+write, and workflows read; minimal to limit blast radius if the token is compromised
OAuth app token covering all public repositories owned by the organization
Personal access token (PAT) with repo and workflow scopes for the service account user
questions.explanation: The GitHub App uses a minimal fine-grained installation token: issues, PRs, contents, and workflows (read). This limits the damage if the short-lived token leaks, and the app is never added to the branch-protection bypass list.

questions.question: What prevents the agent from writing to .github/workflows files, and why is this important?
options: The GitHub App is denied the workflows:write scope, which blocks all writes under .github/workflows at the API level
GitHub App permissions are not path-scoped, so the worker enforces an allow-list on proposed diffs that blocks edits to .github/workflows
Branch protection rules prevent any commit touching workflow files from being pushed
The agent's system prompt includes an instruction to never edit CI configuration files
questions.explanation: GitHub App permissions are coarse-grained, not path-scoped. The worker itself enforces an allow-list on the proposed diff before pushing, blocking any edits under .github/workflows regardless of what the agent proposes.

questions.question: What is 'environment inference' in the context of this capstone?
options: The agent reading environment variables from the repo's .env files to understand configuration
Automatically detecting the repo's language and package manager to generate a Dockerfile for the sandbox if one does not already exist
Using tree-sitter to infer the coding style and formatting conventions before making edits
Sampling the CI logs to infer which tests are flaky before running the full suite
questions.explanation: Environment inference means detecting the language (Python, Node, Go, Rust) and package manager (uv, pnpm, go mod, cargo) from the repo structure, then generating a Dockerfile on the fly if none exists, so the sandbox can build the project from scratch.

questions.question: What gate must pass before the PR is opened, and what happens if coverage regresses?
options: Human code review approval; the PR opens as a draft until a reviewer approves
Full CI must pass in-sandbox; if coverage drops more than 2%, the PR opens but is labeled needs-review
At least 80% of tests must pass; the remaining 20% may be known-flaky tests
The agent must complete within $5 and 15 turns; otherwise the PR is not opened
questions.explanation: The verification gate requires full CI to be green in-sandbox before opening any PR. If CI is red, no PR opens. If coverage drops more than 2%, the PR opens but with a needs-review label signaling that the human reviewer should check it closely.

questions.question: What per-repo budget constraints does the dispatcher enforce?
options: 1 PR per repo per week and $50 per PR
A maximum of 5 PRs per repo per day and $20 per PR
30 agent turns per PR and $10 per day total across all repos
2 concurrent workers per repo and $100 per month total
questions.explanation: The dispatcher enforces per-repo daily ceilings: at most 5 PRs per repo per day and at most $20 per PR, preventing runaway costs from a single busy or broken repository.
